newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal rightist crisis, opposition leader quits.
newsitem.headline: Portugal rightist crisis, opposition leader quits.

text.p: The resignation of the leader of the opposition Popular Party (PP) underlines a deep crisis in right-wing politics in Portugal, political analysts said on Wednesday.

Manuel Monteiro, a lanky 34-year old lawyer, quit as party leader on Tuesday night as his party was being torn apart by his rivalry with a firebrand former newspaper editor, Paulo Portas, and called an extraordinary congress to elect his successor.
"Total war in the PP," ran the banner headline in Diario de Noticias newspaper. "PP without bosses," said Publico.
The PP, unenthusiastic about European integration, is the third largest party in the 230-seat parliament with 15 seats.
The ruling Socialists, who are four seats short of an absolute majority, have 112 seats and the centre-right Social Democratic Party (PSD) have 88.
"The war within the PP underlines a crisis in the right, which extends to the PSD," said Carlos Magno, political commentator with TSF radio.

Political analysts said the PSD led by Marcelo Rebelo de Sousa were struggling to assert their identity in opposition after more than a decade in power before losing last October's general elections to the Socialists led by Antonio Guterres.
"Europe is an issue where the PSD's policies are indistinguishable from the government. The PSD is trying to carve out an identity on that," said a Western diplomat.

Monteiro quit as the PP's leader after four years in charge mainly because of a personality clash with Portas, rather than for any major internal policy differences, although Portas is considered more "Eurosceptical" than Monteiro, analysts said.

Monteiro, an autocratic figure who articulated his party's policies clearly, led the PP to triple its seats in the October election, boosting its share of the vote to nine percent from four percent at the 1991 election.
The PP wants to hold a referendum on revision of the Maastricht treaty, criticises the border-free Schengen agreement and says it would tighten regulations on agricultural imports.

Monteiro's resignation came a day after Portas, the only candidate for the leadership of the PP's parliamentary group, withdrew his candidacy after eight of his colleagues abstained and only seven voted for him.
Five PP MPs, including Portas, later suspended their parliamentary mandates to protest against the lack of solidarity within the party for his candidacy.

Monteiro challenged Portas to stand for the party leadership at the congress which he said should take place after October 13 when regional elections on Portugal's semi-autonomous islands of Madeira and the Azores are due to take place.
The future role of Monteiro in the PP was unclear, although he would have difficulty working with Portas if he were elected, analysts said.
An eventual alliance between some members of the PP and the PSD was possible, they added.
